w: Rising 83 metres above Quito's historic center, this Roman Catholic basilica towers over the old town's rooftops -- a neo-Gothic landmark that dominates the skyline for kilometers around, even without a famous relic inside to draw the crowds.
_facts: Roman Catholic church in the historic center of Quito
reaches up to 83m in height

n: Basilica and Convent of San Francisco
w: Nicknamed 'El Escorial of the New World', this sprawling Franciscan complex is Ecuador's oldest and most significant religious site -- thirteen cloisters and three temples across 3.5 hectares, holding over 3,500 works of colonial art. The entire Quito School of art was born inside these walls.
s: El Escorial of the New World, transplanted to the Andes.
_facts: oldest and most significant religious site in Ecuador
largest architectural complex within historic centers of South America, called El Escorial of the New World
thirteen cloisters, three temples, 3.5 hectares
more than 3,500 works of colonial art
birthplace of the Colonial Quito School of Art

w: Its facade is carved entirely from volcanic stone and its interior sheathed floor to ceiling in gold leaf -- earning La Compania the nicknames 'Temple of Solomon of South America' and, from one awestruck Jesuit traveler, 'Golden Ember'. Two popes have prayed here: John Paul II in 1985, Francis in 2015.
s: A church carved from volcanic rock, gilded in gold.
_facts: facade entirely carved in volcanic stone
called Temple of Solomon of South America and Golden Ember
interior completely covered with gold sheets
visited by Pope John Paul II in 1985 and Pope Francis in 2015

w: Long before the conquest, this loaf-shaped hill was Yavirac, topped -- so the Jesuit historian Juan de Velasco recorded -- by a temple where locals worshipped the sun until Spanish conquistadors tore it down. A 41-metre aluminum Virgin stands on the summit now: taller than Rio's Christ the Redeemer.
s: A sun temple, toppled; a giant Virgin in its place.
_facts: 200m-high volcanic hill, original name Yavirac
per Jesuit historian Juan de Velasco, a temple to the sun stood here until destroyed by Spanish conquistadors
Virgin of El Panecillo statue on the summit is 41m tall including base, tallest statue in Ecuador, taller than Christ the Redeemer in Rio, tallest aluminum statue in the world

w: Quito's central square remembers 10 August 1809, the 'first cry of independence' from Spanish rule, with a monument to the uprising's heroes. Around its edges stand the Carondelet Palace, seat of Ecuador's government, the Metropolitan Cathedral, the Archbishop's Palace and the Municipal Palace.
s: Where Quito first cried for independence, 1809.
_facts: principal central public square of Quito
monument to independence heroes of 10 August 1809, the first cry of independence of the Royal Audience of Quito from Spain
flanked by Carondelet Palace (seat of government), Metropolitan Cathedral, Archbishop's Palace, Municipal Palace

w: Founded in 1873, this is one of the oldest observatories in South America, and one of the most improbably sited -- just 12 minutes south of the Equator, tucked inside Quito's historic center. It became Ecuador's national observatory after passing to the National Polytechnic School in 1963.
s: South America's oldest observatory, on the equator.
_facts: founded 1873, one of the oldest observatories in South America
located 12 minutes south of the Equator in the Historic Center of Quito
national observatory of Ecuador
transferred to National Polytechnic School (EPN) in 1963

w: Painter Oswaldo Guayasamin spent his final years building this hilltop chapel as a monument not to God but to humanity -- a purpose-built museum of murals and sculpture charting the suffering and violence of Latin America. He died before it was finished; it opened in 2002, exactly as he'd envisioned.
s: A chapel built to humanity, not to God.
_facts: purpose-built art museum by painter Oswaldo Guayasamín in Bellavista, dedicated to the peoples of Latin America
construction began 1995, completed 2002 after his death
exhibits sculptures and murals depicting suffering and violence in Latin America
co-designed with Handel Guayasamín

w: Quito's third-largest park runs along Avenida Patria in the old center -- come the weekend, its paths turn into an open-air exhibition, with the park hosting shows every Saturday and Sunday beneath the trees.
s: Quito's third-biggest park, doubling as a weekend gallery.
_facts: public park along Avenue Patria in the Old Centre part of Quito
third-largest park in the city
hosts exhibitions on the weekend

w: The independence hero Antonio Jose de Sucre never got to grow old in this historic-center mansion -- but his belongings did. The ground floor holds the weapons and military kit of Bolivar's trusted marshal; upstairs, the rooms and furniture sit exactly as he and his wife Mariana Carcelen left them.
s: Marshal Sucre's house, frozen at the moment he left it.
_facts: museum in historic center of Quito, established 1977 by the Ministry of Defence
dedicated to independence hero Antonio José de Sucre and his wife Mariana Carcelén
ground floor holds his weapons and military equipment
second floor has furniture and rooms as they appeared in his time

w: Four centuries of hospital history live behind these Doric-columned colonial walls -- the former San Juan de Dios, Quito's old hospital, restored and reopened in 1998 as a museum charting the city's past across ten exhibition halls. In 2020, 69 artifacts were repatriated from a London collector's estate.
s: A hospital turned museum, plus a repatriated collection.
_facts: museum founded 1998 in the colonial center of Quito
occupies former San Juan de Dios Hospital buildings, restored 1995
Doric stone columns and doorways
chronicles Quito's history plus 400 years of the hospital's history, 10 exhibition halls
in July 2020, 69 artifacts privately restituted to Ecuador, originally taken by a London diplomat/collector in the 1960s

w: Behind a 20th-century facade sits a building dating to 1622 that has been, in turn, Quito's first university and a Spanish colonial jail -- one where insurgents were executed during Ecuador's war of independence. Since 1997 it's been a cultural center, its darker history folded quietly into the walls.
s: A 1622 building: university, jail, gallows, now gallery.
_facts: established 1997 as a cultural center, building dates to 1622
facade rebuilt in the 20th century
housed the First Central University
was a jail where Spanish authorities executed insurgents during the Ecuadorian War of Independence

w: A glass pavilion crowns this hill above old Quito -- the Centro Cultural Itchimbia, part exhibition hall, part museum, run today by a private environmental consortium rather than the city. From the top, the view runs west to La Alameda park and the domes of the historic center below.
s: A glasshouse on a hilltop, over Quito's rooftops.
_facts: hill on the eastern/northeastern edge of downtown Quito
hilltop park (Parque Itchimbía) run by private environmentalist corporation Consorcio Ciudad-Ecogestión
glass house on the summit, Centro Cultural Itchimbía, houses an exhibition center, conference room and museum
La Alameda park with the old astronomical observatory lies just west
